title: Hooks: running checks automatically
objective: By the end of this lesson you can run a check before every commit, and you know the limit of what a local hook can be trusted to enforce.

blocks.text: A hook is a script Git runs at a particular moment. The most useful one runs just before a commit is created and can refuse it. That turns a rule everyone agreed to remember into a rule the machine applies.

blocks.caption: Where they live
lines: # Remove the .sample suffix and make it executable to activate one.
# Note: .git/hooks is NOT part of the repository — see the end of this lesson.

rows: Format, lint, run fast tests, block obvious mistakes

blocks.caption: .git/hooks/pre-commit
lines: # 1. Refuse leftover debugging markers in staged changes
echo 'Remove the debugging lines above before committing.' >&2
[ "$size" -gt 5000000 ] && { echo "$f is over 5MB — is it generated?" >&2; exit 1; }

blocks.title: Keep the pre-commit hook fast
blocks.text: A commit is something people do many times an hour. A hook that takes thirty seconds will be bypassed with --no-verify within a day, and then it protects nothing. Put the fast checks here and the slow suite in pre-push or CI.

blocks.caption: Two facts about local hooks
lines: git commit --no-verify -m "..."     # skips pre-commit and commit-msg entirely
# And .git/hooks is not committed, so a fresh clone has NO hooks at all.

blocks.title: A local hook is a helpful reminder, not a control
blocks.text: It can be skipped with one flag and does not exist in a new clone until someone installs it. Anything that genuinely must not enter the shared branch — secrets, failing tests, unreviewed changes — has to be enforced on the server, where nobody can pass --no-verify. Hooks catch mistakes; server-side rules enforce policy.

blocks.caption: Commit them, then point Git at them
lines: # write your hooks there and commit them
# Each person still runs that config line once — record it in the README,
# or run it from your project's setup script.

blocks.text: core.hooksPath is the plain solution: the hooks live in the repository, so they are versioned and reviewed like any other code. Tool-managed alternatives exist for various ecosystems, and they all do the same thing underneath.
What belongs in a hook, and what does not

rows: Formatting and linting the staged files
The full test suite — too slow
Anything the team must not be able to skip
A fast unit subset for the touched area

blocks.title: Write a hook and watch it stop you
steps: In ~/git-lab: printf '#!/bin/sh\nif git diff --cached | grep -q "DO-NOT-COMMIT"; then echo "blocked" >&2; exit 1; fi\n' > .git/hooks/pre-commit
Run: echo 'DO-NOT-COMMIT experiment' > risky.txt && git add risky.txt
Run: git commit -m "Try it"        (blocked — the hook refused)
Run: git commit --no-verify -m "Bypassed"   (it goes through — this is the limit)
Move it into the repository: mkdir -p .githooks && cp .git/hooks/pre-commit .githooks/ && git config core.hooksPath .githooks
blocks.expected: A commit refused by your own rule, the same commit succeeding with --no-verify, and the hook moved into the repository so a colleague can get it. Seeing the bypass work is the point: it is why the real gate lives on the server.

cheatsheet: A hook is a script Git runs at a moment in its lifecycle
pre-commit: format, lint, fast checks, block obvious mistakes
commit-msg: enforce a message convention · pre-push: the slower suite
Keep pre-commit fast, or people will bypass it
.git/hooks is not committed — a fresh clone has none
Share hooks by committing them and setting core.hooksPath
Hooks catch mistakes; only server-side rules enforce policy

checkpoint.prompt: Why can a pre-commit hook not be relied on to keep secrets out of a shared repository?

choices.B: It can be skipped with --no-verify and does not exist in a fresh clone until someone installs it
choices.C: Hooks only run on the default branch
choices.D: Hooks run after the commit is created

checkpoint.explanation: It is a local convenience, not a control. Anything that must not enter the shared branch has to be enforced where the contributor cannot bypass it.

checkpoint.prompt: Your pre-commit hook takes 40 seconds. What is the likely outcome?

choices.A: People commit less often, which is fine
choices.B: People start passing --no-verify, and the hook stops protecting anything

checkpoint.explanation: A check people route around is worse than no check, because it creates the belief that something is being checked. Move slow work to pre-push or CI.

checkpoint.prompt: How do you make hooks available to everyone on the team?

choices.B: Commit them to a tracked directory and set core.hooksPath to it
choices.D: Hooks are shared automatically on clone

checkpoint.explanation: .git/hooks is not part of the repository. A tracked directory plus core.hooksPath makes hooks versioned and reviewable like any other code.

checkpoint.prompt: Which check belongs in CI rather than in pre-commit?

choices.B: The full test suite that takes several minutes

checkpoint.explanation: Pre-commit should be fast enough to be invisible. Long-running suites belong where they do not stand between a person and their commit.
